# Compacted Summary: Chapters 1–35 (Updated 2026-10-13, Final)

## Setting and Time
- **Current Period**: Autumn of ninth year after Waterloo (1830). Story spans from Sunday, 26th April dinner through Chapter 35 (late evening/near 2 A.M.).
- **Key Locations**: London (Welbeck Street, Grosvenor Square, Abchurch Lane, Beargarden Club, Langham Hotel, Euston Square Railway Station, Bruton Street, Lincoln's Inn, Queen's Gate, Islington); Coventry Island; Queen's Crawley; Coldcombe and Mirecombe farms; Bryngate; Pumpernickel; Ostend; Hampshire ("the Evergreens"); Brussels; Aix-la-Chapelle; Bath and Cheltenham; Carbury Hall; Carbury Chase; Caversham; Sussex; Quenwick; Dunholt village; Salford; Sheepstone; Bungay; Sheep's Acre Farm; Sheepstone Birches; Yarlton; Staveton; Fenmere hill farms; Suffolk; New York; San Francisco; Liverpool; Harrowgate; Mirecombe; Duchess of Stevenage's residence; Lady Gamut's residence; Salwick.

## Major Deaths
- **John Sedley, Mr. Osborne, Joseph Sedley, Colonel Rawdon Crawley, Sir Pitt**: All deceased as previously documented.

## Rebecca's Arc
- Never became Lady Crawley; styles herself so. Son (Sir Rawdon, young baronet) receives liberal allowance but declines to see her. Appears very wealthy at Bath and Cheltenham. Busies herself in piety and Charity Lists.

## Amelia and William Dobbin
- Married at Dike (Ostend); Amelia initiated encounter in "dripping white bonnet and shawl." Dobbin quit service, rented "the Evergreens" (Hampshire). Devoted father; fonder of daughter Jane than of his History of the Punjaub.

## Lady Carbury and Family

**Lady Carbury**: Lives on Welbeck Street with Felix and Henrietta. Authored "Criminal Queens." Crushed by "Evening Pulpit" review by Mr. Jones (Mr. Alf's reviewer); praised by "Morning Breakfast Table" review by Mr. Broune. Suspects Alf orders hostile reviews of friends' works. Proposed scheme: if Henrietta married Roger, Felix could inherit Roger's name, title, property. Felix consented to remain at Manor House. At Monday Caversham dinner, found Melmotte "heavy on her hands." Urged Felix to formally propose to Melmotte, warning of slips "between the cup and the lip." Late Chapter 34: Counseled Felix to elope with Marie Melmotte immediately, assuring him "there would be very little" risk; emphasized Melmotte would forgive her and provide settlement; family will "starve unless something be done"; noted Marie "is of age." Chapter 35: Took bull by horns; without telling anyone, wrote pretty note to Melmotte inviting him to Tuesday evening drawing-room. Melmotte (or Miles Grendall) accepted. Tuesday evening: Melmotte arrived; Lady Carbury guided him graciously, mentioned Caversham friends, rushed to discuss "Pulpit" article praising his greatness. Introduced Melmotte to editor Mr. Alf (whom Melmotte had already entertained). Attempted to introduce Melmotte to Mr. Broune (editor of "Breakfast Table," managing morning paper—"heavier burden" than afternoon publication, his commercial articles deemed "gospel"). Before leaving, Melmotte told Lady Carbury: "Your son has proposed to my daughter. My daughter is engaged to another man." Offered: if Felix withdraws, "I'll see that he does uncommon well in the city. I'll be the making of him." Lady Carbury found Melmotte rude but forgave this if gain could follow. Recognized Melmotte prefers lord son-in-law but would likely accept marriage once effected. Lying had become her nature. **Late Chapter 35 (after 2 A.M.): Mr. Broune proposed marriage to her. Word "wife" came as thunderclap, changing her feelings entirely. She did not dream of loving him; was sure she never could. She had looked upon him as intellect, alloyed by passionless remnants of vices; found instead he had human heart she could touch. Asked him to leave due to lateness and Felix's return. Promised to write answer by Thursday. Upon his departure, Felix arrived from club, nearly drunk, stumbling upstairs. Lady Carbury reflects: regardless of Felix's fortune, if he brings her to ruin, she could endure Bohemian life on earnings; Felix is not tyrant who could command her. Marriage vows do not recommend themselves to her. Considers: if Felix goes to dogs, Broune would not want her; if Felix rises in metropolis, neither Felix nor she would want Broune. Liberty matters most.**

**Felix Carbury**: Beautiful; cynosure of mother's eyes. Won £2,000 from Lord Grasslough, £400 from Miles Grendall at gaming. Director of South Central Pacific and Mexican Railway Company. Thursday evening (Chapter 34): Went to Grosvenor Square as Marie desired. Found Melmotte, Lord Nidderdale, Marquis of Auld Reekie, Madame Melmotte, Miss Longestaffe, and Marie in drawing-room. When Melmotte's step ascended, Madame Melmotte screamed "C'est lui" and fled. Felix and Marie alone momentarily; Felix kissed Marie's lips. She said "Now be brave...and I'll be brave." Melmotte entered, asked "Where are the others?" and commanded: "Go away, and don't come back any more...You can't both marry her. I'm not the man to give my daughter a single shilling if she marries against my consent." Yet offered if Felix gives up: "I'll be proud to co-operate with you in anything you may wish to have done in the city." Felix left; woman (Madame Didon) shoved note into his hand. Chapter 34 (late): Contemplated elopement scheme; has sufficient money; considered asking Herr Vossner where to take Marie. Reflected on settlement: even if obtained (likely £50,000 or more), not very much; Melmotte might make possession uncomfortable. Deep waters, but Felix liked them despite discomfort. **Chapter 35 (late): Returned to mother's house from club, nearly drunk, stumbled upstairs. Stated editor fellow (Mr. Broune) was at door; called him "great ass." Assured mother he was "all right."**

**Henrietta Carbury**: Rejected Roger's suit, claiming too young and age disparity insurmountable. Within week, Paul returned "as a still dear friend," promising not to see her three months. Wore rose from Roger's room. When met Roger at door, there was "more in her eyes of graciousness towards him than he had ever seen there before." Roger declared love anew (Chapter 32 evening); Henrietta has not committed; Roger's determination remains unshaken. Paul Montague is thoroughly in love with her.

## Ruby Ruggles
- Granddaughter of old Daniel Ruggles, of Sheep's Acre, parish of Sheepstone, near Bungay. Pretty with long glossy ringlets, large round dark eyes, clear dark complexion; strong, healthy, tall; possessed own will. Had been to marry John Crumb (marriage abandoned/postponed). Understood degradation must be avoided. After Sunday meeting with Felix, resolved: "I suppose I am to be his wedded wife...I'll never be nothing unless I'm that." **Note: Felix prefers Ruby Ruggles as companion in love-making business to Marie Melmotte.**

## The Melmottes

**Augustus Melmotte**: Chairman of South Central Pacific and Mexican Railway Company. Arrived London from Paris within two years; claims English birth but speaks with accent betraying "long expatriation." Big man with large whiskers, rough hair; expression of mental power on harsh vulgar face. In City, his name "worth any money." Taken up old Longestaffe's affairs; has Caversham and Sussex property. Miles Grendall serves as usher/secretary. By Chapter 33 Board day, has twice sold fifty shares at £112 10s., receiving cheques for £625 each (£25 profit per share above £100 nominal). During Whitsun week country visit, remained in summer-house with Lord Alfred, smoking, drinking brandy and seltzer, appearing not in good humour. Chapter 34: Is negotiating to purchase Pickering property from Sir Merton Longestaffe. Thursday evening at Grosvenor Square: Entered drawing-room, asked "Where are the others?" Commanded Felix: "Go away, and don't come back any more." Stated will not give Marie "a single shilling if she marries against my consent." Yet offered if Felix gives up: "I'll be proud to co-operate with you in anything you may wish to have done in the city." Chapter 35: Attended Lady Carbury's Tuesday evening party. Had entertained Mr. Alf previously. Conversation with Mr. Broune (morning paper editor) limited to "Very hot indeed." Before departing, told Lady Carbury: "Your son has proposed to my daughter. My daughter is engaged to another man...If he'll signify to my daughter that he withdraws...I'll see that he does uncommon well in the city. I'll be the making of him." **Believed by Montague to be "as vile a scoundrel as ever lived."**

**Marie Melmotte**: Speaks English well; has begun forming own opinions. Rejected Lord Grasslough; has experience with Lord Nidderdale. Sunday: Fell asleep in chair before fire. Secretly instructed Felix to find father in book-room. Resolved on constancy toward Felix; rejected other suitors. Felt complete happiness; promised to tell mother. Chapter 34: Attending Duchess of Stevenage's dinner and Lady Gamut's musical party. Sent mid-week note to Felix expressing will never take anyone but man she loves (Felix). Thursday evening at Grosvenor Square: Present in drawing-room. When Madame Melmotte fled at Melmotte's arrival, Felix and Marie alone for one moment; Marie lifted up face; Felix kissed her lips. She said "Now be brave...and I'll be brave." After Felix left, Marie delivered note to him via woman in hall. Note reveals: Papa settled money on her in France during visit (amount unknown); cannot be undone without her leave; she refused to give Felix up to father; father declared will not give her anything if she marries without his consent; she is confident he cannot take settlement away and tells Felix because "I think I ought to tell you everything." **Chapter 35: Marie is now engaged to another man (Lord Nidderdale, not Felix).**

**Madame Melmotte**: Gracious as usual but never very gracious. Called Miss Longestaffe "a great bore" and "fatigante." Dismissed Marie's declarations of caring. Appears to know of Felix's offer; does not absolutely disapprove. Thursday evening at Grosvenor Square: When Melmotte's step heard ascending, screamed "C'est lui," hurried out by side door.

## The Longestaffes

**Sir Merton Longestaffe**: Determined no more London expenses that year; family will not return from Caversham. Desires to sell Pickering and disembarrass Caversham from debt. Dolly refused to consent unless half produce given to him. Broke promise to Georgiana of returning to London. Chapter 34: Received letter from Dolly like a thunderbolt that Melmottes must be "very bad indeed,--worse than he had thought." Most angered by passage telling him he ought to have taken family back to town. Is negotiating sale of Pickering to Melmotte.

**Georgiana Longestaffe**: Made strong protest against Melmottes; threatened to stay in London. Father refused; she felt "treachery." Following morning, Lady Pomona handed her undated invitation from Melmotte to stay with them. Expressed contempt for Melmottes, calling them vulgar. Yet concluded: "I'll go." By Sunday, present at Grosvenor Square drawing-room with Madame Melmotte, Marie, and Lord Nidderdale, carrying on flirtation with Nidderdale in half whisper. Chapter 34: Now staying with Melmottes in Grosvenor Square. Dependent on Madame Melmotte for carriage outings and access to social parties. Attending Duchess of Stevenage's dinner and Lady Gamut's musical party. Angry at being left alone by family. Present Thursday evening in Grosvenor Square drawing-room.

**Adolphus (Dolly) Longestaffe**: Has own rooms in Bruton Street; seldom dines with family. Obdurate regarding his own rights in property dealings. Chapter 34: Called on sister at Melmotte house early afternoon. Georgiana complained of confinement. Within last half hour received letter from lawyer regarding Pickering sale negotiations. States his governor wants to sell Pickering; Melmotte wants to buy. His father cannot sell without his consent. Has asked for half the plunder (over and above £50,000 price, above debt on property); £25,000 would pay off what he owes on his own property and make him "very square." Expects father to give in to his terms. Expressed reluctance about property going to pieces. States Melmotte knows all about it; offers to go with Felix to city to-morrow and make it straight about what Felix owes him. Says Melmotte will advance him £1,000, allowing Felix to get railway shares. Mid-week: Dined with Felix at Beargarden; Miles Grendall dining alone at next table; spoke frequently with Grendall but Felix would not join conversation. In smoking-room afterward, asked Felix "Is there anything up between you and Miles?" Felix said no and promised to tell him "all about it in the cab to-morrow." Agreed with Felix on plan to visit Abchurch Lane next day; after negotiation, settled on 2 P.M. departure time from club.

## South Central Pacific and Mexican Railway Scheme

**The Enterprise**: Railway from Salt Lake City, branching from San Francisco and Chicago line, passing through New Mexico and Arizona into Mexico, terminating at Vera Cruz. Approximately 2,000 miles.

**Financial Strategy**: Stock at par; shares sold at premium to "run them up even to 110," yielding three hundred thousand dollars minimum. Directors understood fortune made by floating shares, not making actual railway.

**London Directorate**: Melmotte (chairman), Lord Alfred Grendall, Sir Felix Carbury, Samuel Cohenlupe (MP for Staines), Lord Nidderdale, Paul Montague.

## Paul Montague and Mrs. Winifrid Hurtle

**Paul's Situation**: Living at Beargarden. Junior member of railway firm; English. Personally dislikes Fisker. Trembles for his money. Thoroughly in love with Hetta Carbury; not in love with Mrs. Hurtle. Would have given much golden prospects to have her "reconveyed suddenly to San Francisco." Yet has delight in her presence. Of natural disposition to have strongest affinities and sympathies with women; rarely altogether happy when removed from their influence. Only Hetta herself serves as confidant. Cannot leave Hurtle without seeing her, convinced of her solitude and dependence on him.

**Mrs. Winifrid Hurtle**: Formerly betrothed to Paul. Arrived night before last (Tuesday reached Liverpool, came to London Wednesday). During earlier engagement, promised to follow him. He saw her in New York on second journey to San Francisco, renewed promises. Since then never met until Chapter 34. Has now followed him to London. She said: "I could not get across to San Francisco as I said I would, and when I was there you had quarrelled with your uncle and returned." Theatre Evening: Paul took her to theatre. She commented on acting, addressed play's portrayal of woman crying because lover talked to another woman, noting position described was nearly her own; spoke "on purpose,--fighting her own battle after her own fashion." After theatre, declined Paul's offer to accompany her in cab to Islington but Paul accompanied her anyway. She continued talking during journey. Remarked on London's immensity and dirt; compared New York (bigger than Paris but pleasanter). Called Paris "gem of gems among towns." Stated she did not like Frenchmen, liked Englishmen better than Americans, but fancied could never like English women. "I do so hate all kinds of buckram. I like good conduct, and law, and religion too if it be not forced down one's throat; but I hate what your women call propriety. I suppose what we have been doing to-night is very improper; but I am quite sure that it has not been in the least wicked." Thinks in solitude: He should marry her or world should hear the story of his perjury. Questions whether he, greatly inferior to herself intellectually and in person, should throw her over. Believes he promised to marry her.

## Lord Nidderdale
Intent on marrying Marie Melmotte for her fortune. Claims not afraid of Melmotte, believing he "rather likes me, because I've always been on the square with him." **Chapter 35: Marie is now engaged to Nidderdale (not Felix).** Thursday evening at Grosvenor Square: Present in drawing-room with his father, the Marquis of Auld Reekie.

## Mr. Broune
Editor of "Morning Breakfast Table" (managing morning paper—"heavier burden" than afternoon publication). His commercial articles deemed "gospel." Nearer fifty than sixty; young of his age; can walk four or five miles pleasantly; can ride cob in park with free air as any man of forty; can work through four or five hours of night with easy steadiness. **Chapter 35 (late evening): Came to Lady Carbury's drawing-room with air of perturbation. Rose to feet repeatedly in agitation. After much thought, determined to ask her to be his wife. Stated "we are neither of us so young as we used to be." She felt sure she never could love him; viewed him as friend to be used because he knew world; now found he had human heart she could touch. Mixed with other feelings was tenderness bringing memory of distant youth, almost making her weep. She asked him to leave due to lateness and Felix's return. Promised to write answer by Thursday. Took her hand, kissed it, left without another word. As he opened front door to let himself out, Felix (returning from club, nearly drunk) entered house. Felix greeted him with mingled impudence and surprise, calling him "old fellow" and commenting he'd "been keeping it up late." Broune passed Felix without word. As he went to work, endeavoured to bathe himself in self-complacency; but at bottom was substratum of melancholy which leavened his prospects.**

## Roger Carbury
Nearly forty years old. Never owed shilling he could not pay; father likewise. Firmly opposed to Melmotte connection on principle. Took degree at Oxford; became "pervert," supposed "convert." Works as priest earning day-labourer's wages; forced to buy second-hand clothes. Soft heart; knows Lady Carbury false and Felix worthless, yet condemns himself for harsh words. During Sunday evening with Father Barham, engaged in theological debate; became tired of priest's intolerance. Declared love to Henrietta anew (Chapter 32 evening); determination remains unshaken. Is rival for Henrietta's affection with Paul Montague.

## Father John Barham
Priest of Beccles. Dogmatic Catholic; believes man should abandon reason to care of another or others. In county only twelve months.

## Property Relations
**Daniel Ruggles' Land**: Holds Sheep's Acre Farm on bishop's lease, part of property which belonged to bishopric of Elmham. Also holds small extent of outlying meadow belonging to Carbury estate; thus one of Roger Carbury's tenants.

## Other Characters
- **Miles Grendall**: Secretary/usher to Melmotte. Does not pay debts of honour. Sunday card-room: Won heavily, particularly from Paul Montague; received considerable ready money "quite a godsend to him." When pressed by Felix about debt, rose and suggested billiards, walking slowly out of room. During hour of play, observed moving chair farther from Felix and nearer to Dolly. Chapter 34: Mid-week at Beargarden, dined alone at table next to Felix and Dolly; spoke frequently with Dolly but never addressed Felix, nor did Felix join conversation; Dolly noticed distance.
- **Lord Grasslough**: Present at Sunday card-room gambling.
- **Marquis of Auld Reekie**: Lord Nidderdale's father. Fierce-looking, gouty old man with watery eyes and stiff grey-white hair. Supporting himself on two sticks. Thursday evening at Grosvenor Square: Proposed Felix go downstairs with him; Felix resisted, citing Melmotte's house.
